title: GTA 6: The female gamers crushing moral panic about Grand Theft Auto
transcript:
Speaker 1: From The Australian, this is the weekend edition of The Front. I'm Claire Harvey. Grand Theft Auto is one of the biggest video game franchises in the world, and this week saw the release of GTA 6, its most anticipated instalment yet. On the surface, the concept of Grand Theft Auto sounds surprisingly bland. Instead of, say, boarding a spaceship and battling aliens in far-off galaxies, players drive around virtual versions of real world cities like New York, Miami and LA. But in GTA, the hook isn't escaping to other worlds. It's getting to be someone else, the bad guy. GTA is not just a cultural story. It's a huge business moment with sales expected to soar past $ 3 billion in the first week alone. It's also a story about world building and moral panic. Today, the Australian's National Chief of Staff, Sarah Ison, joins me to break down the appeal of breaking the law in the Grand Theft Auto universe. GTA came out in 1997. I don't think you were 18 plus back then.
Speaker 2: I wasn't 18 plus. I think I got in at like San Andreas, so 2004 that was released. So kind of early high school was when I started to get into it. playing on the PlayStation 2, you know, it's the same era as Need for Speed. So yeah, it was definitely something I played quite a lot when I was a kid.
Speaker 1: And what had been your gaming journey up till then?
Speaker 2: My gaming journey, I think it sort of was, I don't know, Ratchet and Clank, Jak and Daxter, like some really more fantasy sort of games that don't really have a lot of semblance to real life. that aren't really as first person or not really open world. So that's why it was so striking because GTA was all of those things. in terms of how open world it was, that you were really feeling like a real person, you were getting in a car, you were driving through traffic lights or whatever, and for like a 13, 14-year-old, oh, I mean 18, you, yeah, it felt really different.
Speaker 1: It must have felt kind of edgy and cool as well.
Speaker 2: Like getting ready for school with your tie and your blazer and your coho and being like, I'm going to rob some banks, you know. Hand over every last dollar!
Speaker 1: Now, bitch! I'm going to empty the safe! Keep these idiots covered! And did your mum and dad know what was going on?
Speaker 2: No, I don't know. I think at that age, my brother and I would just like, you know, get games off friends kind of thing. Yeah, it wasn't something that mum and dad ever seemed to have any concerns about, I guess. It was just Sam and I, my brother and I having a lot of fun and a lot of laughs, I guess, in the games room.
Speaker 1: By then, in game years, GTA was already kind of quite old.
Speaker 2: I know. I couldn't believe some of the looking back at where it started.
Speaker 1: 1997, the year that Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone came out as a book. Good Will Hunting came out that year. The release of GTA was a cultural moment, a bit like the launch of Harry Potter. Like, it has changed the world, probably. Certainly changed gaming. And a bit like Harry Potter, there was a moral panic about it at the time, much more intense than the Christians who were objecting to Harry Potter being about witchcraft, believe it or not. This is a true representation of witchcraft. And yet we have people that say this is merely fantasy and harmless reading for our children. Every release of GTA has triggered the same kind of concerns, maybe except this one. A new study has revealed gaming addictions affects children's behaviour and their self-esteem. It's almost routine in popular games for players to spray other people with Uzis, to drive over pedestrians, to kill police officers. to attack women. What do you think about that? And what was that like when you got into the game?
Speaker 2: Well, I feel like there definitely were some questions that I almost have retrospectively, like for the 2004 game, who you could essentially kill and so on. It was pretty intense. And I was surprised with this new game that was released that A lot of the reporting I've seen around it hasn't brought a lot of that up. It's also moved from you being an African-American man sort of in the hood, as he would call it, and that sort of could be derogatory in some ways. Very problematic. Now you can play a man or a woman.
Speaker 1: Hi, Jason! GTA 6 sees the introduction of a Bonnie and Clyde-style duo. This is a free call from Lucia Caminos. Jason Duvall and Lucia Caminos, giving players their first female protagonist option.
Speaker 2: You know, it's sort of changed in that way. So I think people are seeing it as fundamentally different, but also reflective of the time America is in, like this idea of, oh, this game is awful because of the violence or the crime or the... It's like, well, that's where the country is at. It also has this sense, at least from creators and supporters, it's reflective, it's illustrative of... Come to Phil's AMU Nation today.
Speaker 1: We got more guns than the law allows.
Speaker 2: And to have an outrage or moral panic about it, it's sort of devoid of reality when this is exactly what's going on out there.
Speaker 1: Kids for forever have been playing cops and robbers in some form or other, and someone has to be the robber in that game. I wonder why the gamification of that, the video gamification of it, made us sort of forget that Just because you're playing a robber in an imaginary game, you're not going to become a robber in real life.
Speaker 2: Yeah, I think I guess it's just that thing that's new, right? As with everything, social media or whatever, this idea of you playing something and there's a screen up there and it's relatively realistic and so on. It's just something that people hadn't seen in generations before. And so what that means, what that does to your brain, to all of that, I think that was just raising a lot of questions at the time.
Speaker 1: On this video games affecting our brains say it ain't so well.
Speaker 2: To the great delight of many a lot of games did that for different reasons you have call of duty and others and people talking about the glorification of war and how is this big push and conspiracy that's meant to get more people to enlist because that's how it makes people feel but then i think the longer time has gone on and particularly in the wake of other things happening against social media or ai or whatever it's more muted or it's smaller in comparison than we thought it was going to be, this Armageddon moment, that it hasn't really felt like that. I mean, people can literally access really violent material online or on social media or whatever that is real, that is radicalising kids or whatever. A game made by Rockstar that's this, you know, fictionalised thing, I just think it pales in comparison with that concern.
Speaker 1: If you were 20 when GTA came out in 97, which I was, although I wasn't playing it, I was too busy, you know, drinking cocktails with my friends and kind of dating boys. Although the boys are playing GTA. You are now 50.
Speaker 2: You're about to turn 50.
Speaker 1: Those people are now the establishment. They are running companies. They're sort of editing newspapers. You know, they're the young Gen Xers. And of course, many people who started playing GTA back in 97 would now be 60, 70, 80. Is that why there's not a moral panic this time? Because we've seen those people become sort of upstanding adults and they're not ruining society. Yeah.
Speaker 2: And if they have had kids who then hypothetically get into GTA, it's not that unknown like it was for the parents of kids playing between 97 and the early 2000s. It is a known. And yeah, it is something where they can reflect back on their experience in this game and others and really look at themselves soberly and sort of say, it's just a game.
Speaker 1: The thing that's happened since then is the advent of YouTube and the sharing of kind of playthroughs and walkthroughs of games. So I encountered GTA through my children who watch Mr. Beast and his friends play. We will be playing GTA and breaking zero laws.
Speaker 2: No laws broken today, baby.
Speaker 1: We're following the rules. We're going to give you guys challenges. YouTube has kind of captured that sharing and kind of interactivity, learning from one another. skills development, hasn't it? That previously it would just be you and your brother.
Speaker 2: Yeah. And it's Twitch and so on. It's that shared thing. It's the performative nature of it. You've got people in the corner of the screen having laughs and jokes and so on. It's the kind of cult following around even those gamers and how everything is very live. The comments are rolling live. And if you comment, they're going to read that out online. it feels global, like you're a part of this with all these people. And so, yeah, I think it has expanded that. But I think at its essence, the sort of thing that I see, you know, your Twitch streams and so on, laughing out and people laughing with them, has that nugget of what my brother and I would be laughing about at the time, but streamed to the world.
Speaker 1: What does your generation panic about in the way that my parents' generation panicked about GTA?
Speaker 2: I mean, there's like climate panic and like, oh, the world's going to end soon, kind of jokingly, but not. And then, you know, the online sphere, it's just scary and the stuff you can access online. And I think that means for someone like my age thinking about having a kid, in our parents' generation, it was like, oh, how do I stop my kid from watching TV and stopping that screen time? Like there's no way for you just to turn off the television and say, no, go to your room anymore. Like it's going to be all around them and how do you figure that out?
Speaker 1: Your generation's also so kind of reflective about yourselves and you analyze yourselves and you're very fluent in your own internal language. Like you know yourselves in a way that I don't think my generation did. And you've identified that you're all addicted to your phones just like we all are. And now you're really worried about them. next generation of children, which is really, it's really interesting to see. I see a lot of very worried 20 and 30 year olds about phone use.
Speaker 2: My gen and the younger gen, you see all these things that they're doing to try to manage it. whether it's the dinner where we put our phones in a bag. I went to a dinner in Sydney that that happened recently.
Speaker 1: Really? Yeah. I forget where.
Speaker 2: It's a really fancy place. But, yeah, they asked us for our phones in a bag and I was like, not in this job.
Speaker 1: That's not happening. No, no, no.
Speaker 2: Oh, yeah, Felbury, Melbourne. So Melbourne.
Speaker 1: So Melbourne. But also if you're a parent or you have an elderly parent at home who needs you.
Speaker 2: Or, you know, like, no thanks. But you can also do this thing where you put on a black and white setting at night. Because the whole thing about phones and social media is the way it's designed is about being addicting and about like, oh, it's the colour, it's the light, it's this. And it's actually quite hard to train your neurology.
Speaker 1: Out of that. The moral panic about GTA definitely didn't come true. Street crime is massively down in the past 30 years. Vehicle theft is massively down in Australia, partly because of the introduction of engine immobilisers in 2001 and then electronic keys. Now there's a different problem, which is people stealing cars for TikTok.
Speaker 2: Yeah, that's so true. Like they're trying to do it for the gram.
Speaker 1: That's terrifying. Yeah, breaking into the house to get the key. But, I mean, I think that is amplified by TikTok. Like that's creating a new kind of panic when actually the risk of that happening to you is minuscule. Yeah. But you can see it on TikTok kind of all day, every day. And so it feels very real. How do you think GTA goes now? It's 30 now. It's about to turn 30. What happens in the sort of second third of GTA's life?
Speaker 2: What I like is the sort of agency where you are really choosing what kind of human or player you want to be.
Speaker 1: I quite like that.
Speaker 2: There's some games that have done this before, Infamous and so on, where your actions do have consequences for how then the game evolves, which I quite like. And so that idea of things not just like happening to you or around you, but that you're changing them, it means that also every player's experience is different. It's not like TikTok where if you and I are watching the same video, we're watching the same video, right? We might have a different sort of response maybe, but that's it. Whereas that's sort of also the joy about a lot of open world games. You playing however many hours you would put into GTA versus mine, apart from like the main storyline, they would look like completely different. That is something that will only continue in GTA and in games more broadly because I think people are looking also for that agency and to shape things as well as opposed to things just happening to them and things to witness.
Speaker 1: Thanks, Sarah.
Speaker 2: Thank you.
Speaker 1: Sarah Eisen is The Australian's National Chief of Staff. You can read her work anytime at theaustralian.com.au. Thanks for joining us on The Front this week. I'm Claire Harvey. The Australian's audio lead is Jasper League. Our team also includes Kristen Amiet, Liat Samaglou, Tiffany Dimak and Joshua Burton.
